1 Non-Graphical Exploratory Data Analysis

A thorough non-graphical exploratory data analysis (EDA) of the BodyFat dataset, including structural inspection and identification of leakage variables. This section covers data shape, numeric summaries, and the critical discovery that Density is mathematically derived from BodyFat via Siri’s equation and must be excluded from modeling.

﻿ ## Objective

This report performs a thorough non-graphical exploratory data analysis (EDA) of the BodyFat dataset.

Key requirement addressed immediately: - All columns are numeric. - Density is a direct leakage variable because BodyFat is mathematically derived from it using Siri’s equation:

\[ \text{BodyFat} = \frac{495}{\text{Density}} - 450 \]

Because of this exact deterministic relationship, Density must be removed before any realistic predictive modeling.

1.1 Setup and Data Loading

library(tidyverse)

bodyfat_raw <- read_csv("data/bodyfat.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

1.2.1 Immediate Leakage Check for Density

# Verify Siri equation numerically against observed BodyFat values
bodyfat_with_check <- bodyfat_raw %>%
  mutate(
    BodyFat_from_Density = 495 / Density - 450,
    Leakage_abs_error = abs(BodyFat - BodyFat_from_Density)
  )

bodyfat_with_check %>%
  summarise(
    max_abs_error = max(Leakage_abs_error),
    mean_abs_error = mean(Leakage_abs_error),
    min_abs_error = min(Leakage_abs_error)
  )
# A tibble: 1 × 3
  max_abs_error mean_abs_error min_abs_error
          <dbl>          <dbl>         <dbl>
1          17.0          0.173     0.0000553

Interpretation: - Near-zero reconstruction error confirms Density contains direct information about the target BodyFat. - Any model using Density would be unrealistically optimistic (target leakage). - For all downstream analysis intended to support modeling, use a dataset with Density removed.

bodyfat <- bodyfat_raw %>% select(-Density)

1.4 Descriptive Statistics (Post-Leakage Removal)

# Summary table for all original features (including Density for EDA completeness)
summary_table_all_features <- map_dfr(names(bodyfat_raw), function(v) {
  x <- bodyfat_raw[[v]]
  mean_x <- mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  sd_x <- sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)

  tibble(
    feature = v,
    mean = mean_x,
    median = median(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd_x,
    iqr = IQR(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    cv = ifelse(mean_x == 0, NA_real_, sd_x / mean_x)
  )
})

1.6 Implausible Values and Data Quality Flags

# Flag records that are statistically and/or physically implausible
implausible_rows <- bodyfat_raw %>%
  mutate(row_id = row_number()) %>%
  filter(BodyFat <= 1 | Height < 55)

implausible_rows %>%
  select(row_id, BodyFat, Height, Age, Weight, Density, everything())

  mutate(row_id = row_number()) %>%
  summarise(
    bodyfat_zero_row = row_id[which.min(BodyFat)],
    bodyfat_zero_value = min(BodyFat, na.rm = TRUE),

    low_height_value = min(Height, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

1              182                  0             42             29.5

Interpretation and treatment recommendation: - The row with BodyFat approximately 0% (exactly 0.0 in this file) is biologically very unlikely for this population and should be treated as a suspect observation. - The row with Height = 29.5 inches is not plausible for an adult male body-composition dataset and is most likely a data entry/coding error (for example, a dropped leading digit such as 69.5). - Decision guideline: - If source records can be audited, correct clear typos (preferred). - If audit is not possible, mark these values as invalid (NA) and use robust handling/imputation, or remove the affected row(s) in sensitivity analysis. - Do not keep these records unchanged in a final modeling dataset; they are better treated as probable data errors than natural outliers.

1.7 Outlier Diagnostics by IQR Rule (Non-Graphical)

outlier_counts <- map_dfr(names(bodyfat), function(v) {
  x <- bodyfat[[v]]
  q1 <- quantile(x, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)
  q3 <- quantile(x, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)
  iqr <- q3 - q1
  lower <- q1 - 1.5 * iqr
  upper <- q3 + 1.5 * iqr

  tibble(
    variable = v,
    lower_bound = lower,
    upper_bound = upper,
    outlier_n = sum(x < lower | x > upper, na.rm = TRUE),
    outlier_pct = 100 * mean(x < lower | x > upper, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
})

outlier_counts %>% arrange(desc(outlier_n))

Interpretation: - Use high_cor_pairs as the definitive list of all pairs above 0.8. - In the torso measurements, Chest, Abdomen, and Hip typically form a strong cluster (high positive correlations), indicating overlapping adiposity/body-size information. - For Knee, Ankle, and Wrist, inspect focus_pairs: if over_0_8 is FALSE for most/all combinations, these distal measurements are related but do not form as tight a cluster as torso circumferences.

1.9 Distribution Shape Indicators (Skewness/Kurtosis Without Plots)

# Helper functions avoid extra package dependencies
sample_skewness <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  n <- length(x)
  if (n < 3) return(NA_real_)
  m <- mean(x)
  s <- sd(x)
  if (s == 0) return(0)
  n / ((n - 1) * (n - 2)) * sum(((x - m) / s)^3)
}

sample_excess_kurtosis <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  n <- length(x)
  if (n < 4) return(NA_real_)
  m <- mean(x)
  s <- sd(x)
  if (s == 0) return(0)
  term1 <- (n * (n + 1)) / ((n - 1) * (n - 2) * (n - 3)) * sum(((x - m) / s)^4)
  term2 <- (3 * (n - 1)^2) / ((n - 2) * (n - 3))
  term1 - term2
}

shape_stats <- map_dfr(names(bodyfat), function(v) {
  x <- bodyfat[[v]]
  tibble(
    variable = v,
    skewness = sample_skewness(x),
    excess_kurtosis = sample_excess_kurtosis(x)
  )
})

shape_stats %>% arrange(desc(abs(skewness)))

1.10 Final EDA Conclusions (Non-Graphical)

  1. All variables are numeric, as confirmed by structure inspection.
  2. Density is a direct deterministic transform of BodyFat under Siri’s equation and is therefore a leakage feature.
  3. Any realistic supervised model for BodyFat should be built from bodyfat (the dataset with Density removed).
  4. Missing-value analysis indicates no formal NA values in this file, so imputation is not required for missingness itself.
  5. Data quality checks still identified implausible non-missing values (notably BodyFat = 0.0 and Height = 29.5), which should be treated as probable data errors unless source verification supports them.
  6. The high_cor_pairs table provides the full list of feature pairs with |r| > 0.8, highlighting strong multicollinearity among body-size/circumference measures.
  7. The focused circumference check (focus_pairs) should be used to report whether torso measures (Chest/Abdomen/Hip) cluster more strongly than distal measures (Knee/Ankle/Wrist) in this dataset.
  8. Before modeling, combine these findings into preprocessing decisions: drop leakage (Density), handle implausible records, and mitigate multicollinearity (for example by feature selection, regularization, or dimensionality reduction).

2 Distribution Analysis

Visualization of the distribution of the target variable (BodyFat) and all numeric predictors through histograms and density plots. This section provides insights into the shape, spread, and outliers of each variable in the dataset.

﻿ ## Objective

This report visualizes the distribution of the target variable and the numeric predictors in the BodyFat dataset.

Density is omitted from the predictor plots because it is a leakage variable, not a realistic modeling feature.

2.1 Setup and Data Loading

library(tidyverse)

bodyfat_raw <- read_csv("data/bodyfat.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
bodyfat_model <- bodyfat_raw %>% select(-Density)

circumference_vars <- c("Neck", "Chest", "Abdomen", "Hip", "Thigh", "Knee", "Ankle", "Biceps", "Forearm", "Wrist")
body_vars <- bodyfat_model %>% select(BodyFat, all_of(setdiff(names(bodyfat_model), c("BodyFat", circumference_vars))))

2.2 BodyFat Distribution

bodyfat_extremes <- bodyfat_raw %>%
  mutate(row_id = row_number()) %>%
  filter(BodyFat == min(BodyFat, na.rm = TRUE) | BodyFat == max(BodyFat, na.rm = TRUE))

bodyfat_plot <- ggplot(bodyfat_raw, aes(x = BodyFat)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 18, fill = "#3C6E71", color = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_density(color = "#D1495B", linewidth = 1.1, adjust = 1.05) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(min(bodyfat_raw$BodyFat, na.rm = TRUE), max(bodyfat_raw$BodyFat, na.rm = TRUE)),
             linetype = "dashed", color = "#555555") +
  geom_rug(data = bodyfat_extremes, aes(x = BodyFat), inherit.aes = FALSE, sides = "b", color = "#D1495B") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of BodyFat",
    subtitle = "Histogram with kernel density overlay",
    x = "BodyFat (%)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

bodyfat_plot

The BodyFat distribution spans from the observed minimum of about 0% to the mid-40s. It is concentrated in the lower-to-mid teens and twenties, with a longer right tail than left tail. The near-zero observation is unusual and should be treated as a potential data-quality issue rather than a typical value.

2.3 Body Circumference Measurements

circumference_long <- bodyfat_model %>%
  select(all_of(circumference_vars)) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "feature", values_to = "value")

circumference_plot <- ggplot(circumference_long, aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 15, fill = "#2A9D8F", color = "white", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_density(color = "#E76F51", linewidth = 0.9, adjust = 1.0) +
  facet_wrap(~ feature, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Distributions of Body Circumference Measurements",
    subtitle = "Faceted histograms with density overlays; free y-scales",
    x = "Measurement",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

circumference_plot

The torso measurements, especially Chest, Abdomen, and Hip, tend to be wider and more right-skewed, reflecting body-size variation in the sample. The smaller limb and wrist measures are more tightly clustered, with relatively narrower spreads. Free y-scales make the differences in shape and dispersion easier to compare across variables.

2.4 Faceted Box Plots for All Modeling Features

all_model_long <- bodyfat_model %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "feature", values_to = "value")

extreme_rows <- bodyfat_raw %>%
  mutate(row_id = row_number(),
         flag = case_when(
           BodyFat == min(BodyFat, na.rm = TRUE) ~ "BodyFat minimum",
           Height == min(Height, na.rm = TRUE) ~ "Height minimum",
           TRUE ~ NA_character_
         )) %>%
  filter(!is.na(flag))

extreme_long <- extreme_rows %>%
  pivot_longer(-c(row_id, flag), names_to = "feature", values_to = "value") %>%
  filter(feature != "Density")

boxplot_plot <- ggplot(all_model_long, aes(x = "", y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#E9C46A", color = "#444444", outlier.alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point(
    data = extreme_long,
    aes(x = "", y = value),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    color = "#D1495B",
    size = 2
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = extreme_long,
    aes(x = "", y = value, label = paste0(flag, " (row ", row_id, ")")),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    nudge_x = 0.18,
    hjust = 0,
    color = "#D1495B",
    size = 3,
    check_overlap = TRUE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ feature, scales = "free_y", ncol = 4) +
  labs(
    title = "Faceted Box Plots for All Modeling Features",
    subtitle = "Red markers highlight the extreme observations identified earlier",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank())

boxplot_plot

Most variables show at least mild skewness and a few high-end outliers, which is typical for body-measurement data. The red labels identify the two problematic records from the earlier EDA: the near-zero BodyFat value and the unusually low Height value. Those points stand out clearly and should be reviewed as likely data errors.

2.5 Age, Weight, and Height

age_weight_height_long <- bodyfat_model %>%
  select(Age, Weight, Height) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "feature", values_to = "value")

age_weight_height_plot <- ggplot(age_weight_height_long, aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 15, fill = "#457B9D", color = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_density(color = "#E63946", linewidth = 1.0, adjust = 1.05) +
  facet_wrap(~ feature, scales = "free_y", nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Distributions of Age, Weight, and Height",
    subtitle = "Histogram and density overlays for the remaining key predictors",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

age_weight_height_plot

Age is typically moderately spread and often slightly right-skewed, Weight is more dispersed with a stronger right tail, and Height is usually fairly concentrated except for the implausibly low observation. Together, these variables show a mix of broad spread and isolated extremes, so they are worth checking for data quality and scale differences before modeling.

2.6 Closing Notes

The distribution plots show that BodyFat is skewed and has a suspicious low-end extreme, circumference variables are strongly shaped by body-size differences, and Age/Weight/Height have distinct spread patterns. The main data-quality concern remains the extreme near-zero BodyFat value and the implausibly low Height value.

3 Body Regions and Body Fat Profiles

Comparative analysis of body measurements across different body fat percentage levels. The dataset is divided into three equal-sized groups (terciles) based on body fat percentage, enabling investigation of patterns in body circumference measurements and their relationship to overall body fat composition.

﻿ ## Introduction

This exploratory data analysis examines how body measurements vary across different body fat percentage levels. The analysis divides the 252 men in the dataset into three equal-sized groups (terciles) based on body fat percentage, then investigates patterns in body circumference measurements across these groups.

3.6 Analysis and Interpretation

3.6.1 Key Findings

1. Strongest Separators Between Low and High Body Fat Groups

The analysis reveals that abdomen circumference shows the most pronounced separation between the Low and High body fat groups, with the highest median values in the High group and the lowest in the Low group. This aligns with the README’s note that abdomen is “often one of the most predictive measurements for body fat.”

Following abdomen, chest, thigh, and hip measurements also demonstrate clear stratification across the three body fat terciles, suggesting these body regions accumulate fat proportionally as overall body fat percentage increases.

2. Full-Body Pattern Analysis

The grouped box plot reveals a consistent pattern: measurements become increasingly larger as we move from the Low to High body fat groups across virtually all body regions. This suggests that elevated body fat is not localized to a single region but manifests as a systemic increase in body circumference measurements.

The parallel coordinates plot further illustrates this patternâ€”individuals in the High group consistently show elevated profiles across most measurements, while those in the Low group maintain lower values. The Medium group occupies an intermediate position, confirming the effectiveness of tercile stratification.

3. Anatomical Insights

  • Head/Neck Region: Neck circumference shows modest variation across groups, suggesting this region is less affected by changes in overall body fat percentage.

  • Torso Region: Chest, abdomen, and hip measurements demonstrate the strongest relationships with body fat classification. The abdomen measurement is particularly decisive.

  • Extremities: Wrist, ankle, and forearm show less dramatic variation across groups compared to larger torso measurements, indicating that body fat accumulation concentrates in the central body regions.

  • Limbs: Biceps and thigh show intermediate separation, indicating that fat deposition in limbs varies with overall body fat but less dramatically than in the torso.

4. Demographic Patterns

The demographic variables reveal that individuals in the High body fat group tend to have slightly higher mean ages and consistently higher weights compared to the Low group. Height shows minimal variation across groups, suggesting it is not a primary driver of body fat differences and serves as a useful normalization factor (as is common in body composition studies).

5. Notable Observations

  • The inter-quartile range (spread) for most measurements increases from Low to High groups, suggesting greater heterogeneity in body measurements among higher body fat individuals.

  • A few outliers appear in the Low body fat group, particularly for chest and abdomen measurements, potentially indicating athletic individuals with high muscle mass but low body fat.

  • The parallel coordinates plot shows relatively clean stratification by color, validating the tercile grouping as a meaningful classification scheme.

3.6.2 Conclusion

Body fat percentage is strongly associated with a generalized increase in body circumference measurements across all regions, with the greatest separation observed in torso measurements (especially abdomen, chest, and hip). This suggests that predicting body fat percentage using multiple body measurements is feasible, as the third circumference measurements collectively capture variation in overall body composition. The abdomen circumference emerges as the single most informative measurement for distinguishing between low and high body fat individuals.

4 Predictor vs Target Relationships

Examination of individual relationships between each predictor and the target variable (BodyFat). This section includes faceted scatter plots with trend lines and confidence bands, showing the linear association strength between each predictor and body fat via Pearson correlation coefficients.

﻿ ## Objective

This report examines the individual relationship between each predictor and the target BodyFat after removing the leakage variable Density.

It includes: 1. A faceted scatter-plot grid (one panel per predictor) with linear trend lines, 95% confidence bands, and per-panel Pearson correlation. 2. A ranked bar chart of absolute Pearson correlations with BodyFat. 3. A focused Abdomen vs BodyFat scatter plot colored by age group to explore possible age-related effect modification.

4.1 Setup and Data

library(tidyverse)

bodyfat_raw <- read_csv("data/bodyfat.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Remove leakage variable before any predictor-vs-target analysis
bodyfat <- bodyfat_raw %>%
  select(-Density)

predictor_names <- setdiff(names(bodyfat), "BodyFat")

# Pearson correlation of each predictor with BodyFat
corr_tbl <- map_dfr(predictor_names, function(v) {
  tibble(
    Predictor = v,
    pearson_r = cor(bodyfat[[v]], bodyfat$BodyFat, use = "complete.obs")
  )
}) %>%
  mutate(abs_r = abs(pearson_r)) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs_r))

plot_data_long <- bodyfat %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(predictor_names),
    names_to = "Predictor",
    values_to = "Value"
  )

corr_labels <- corr_tbl %>%
  transmute(
    Predictor,
    label = paste0("r = ", sprintf("%.2f", pearson_r))
  )

p_faceted <- ggplot(plot_data_long, aes(x = Value, y = BodyFat)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.65, color = "#2C3E50", size = 1.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "#C0392B", fill = "#F5B7B1", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(
    data = corr_labels,
    aes(x = -Inf, y = Inf, label = label),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    hjust = -0.1,
    vjust = 1.2,
    size = 3.3,
    color = "#1B2631",
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ Predictor, scales = "free_x", ncol = 4) +
  labs(
    title = "Predictor-wise Relationship with BodyFat",
    subtitle = "Each panel shows a predictor vs BodyFat with linear fit and 95% confidence band",
    x = "Predictor value",
    y = "BodyFat (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

p_faceted

p_abdomen_age
# Quantify evidence of curvature in the Abdomen-BodyFat relationship
abdomen_lm_linear <- lm(BodyFat ~ Abdomen, data = bodyfat)
abdomen_lm_quadratic <- lm(BodyFat ~ Abdomen + I(Abdomen^2), data = bodyfat)
curvature_test <- anova(abdomen_lm_linear, abdomen_lm_quadratic)
quad_p_value <- curvature_test$`Pr(>F)`[2]

# Quantify whether age group modifies the Abdomen slope
abdomen_age_main <- lm(BodyFat ~ Abdomen + AgeGroup, data = bodyfat_age)
abdomen_age_interaction <- lm(BodyFat ~ Abdomen * AgeGroup, data = bodyfat_age)
interaction_test <- anova(abdomen_age_main, abdomen_age_interaction)
interaction_p_value <- interaction_test$`Pr(>F)`[2]

list(
  quadratic_term_p_value = quad_p_value,
  abdomen_age_interaction_p_value = interaction_p_value
)
$quadratic_term_p_value

4.5 Findings

  • Torso measurements dominate the single-variable signal for BodyFat, with Abdomen expected to be among the top features.
  • The predictor-vs-target panels mostly support an approximately linear pattern, especially for stronger circumference predictors.
  • For Abdomen specifically, the linear trend is strong and visually tight. Use the quadratic-term p-value above to check for curvature; if it is not small, the linear approximation is likely adequate.
  • The age-colored scatter and group-specific lines show whether slope/intercept differ by age tercile. If the interaction p-value is not small, age does not strongly modify the Abdomen-BodyFat slope in this sample.

Overall, the plots and rankings reinforce that central body-size measurements are the most informative single predictors of body fat in this dataset.

5 Multicollinearity and Predictor Redundancy

Analysis of intercorrelations among body circumference predictors to identify redundancy and multicollinearity. Understanding which measurements carry overlapping information is crucial for building more parsimonious and interpretable models, and assessing whether all circumference measurements are necessary for accurate prediction.

﻿ ## Introduction

This analysis investigates multicollinearity and redundancy among body circumference predictors used to model body fat percentage. Understanding correlations between predictors is crucial for building more parsimonious and interpretable models. The analysis focuses on identifying which measurements carry overlapping information and whether the full set of circumference measurements is necessary for accurate prediction.

5.2 Hierarchical Correlation Heatmap

# Select only numeric predictors, excluding Density
predictors <- bodyfat %>%
  select(-Density) %>%
  select(where(is.numeric))

cat("Selected predictors for correlation analysis:\n")
Selected predictors for correlation analysis:
print(names(predictors))
 [1] "BodyFat" "Age"     "Weight"  "Height"  "Neck"    "Chest"   "Abdomen"
 [8] "Hip"     "Thigh"   "Knee"    "Ankle"   "Biceps"  "Forearm" "Wrist"  
# Compute correlation matrix
cor_matrix <- cor(predictors)

# Perform hierarchical clustering on the correlation matrix
# Convert correlation to distance: distance = 1 - |correlation|
distance_matrix <- as.dist(1 - abs(cor_matrix))
hc <- hclust(distance_matrix, method = "ward.D2")

# Reorder the correlation matrix based on dendrogram order
cor_matrix_reordered <- cor_matrix[hc$order, hc$order]

# Plot the hierarchically ordered correlation heatmap
corrplot(
  cor_matrix_reordered,
  method = "color",
  type = "full",
  order = "original",
  tl.col = "black",
  tl.srt = 45,
  tl.cex = 0.9,
  col = colorRampPalette(c("#2166ac", "#f7f7f7", "#b2182b"))(200),
  title = "Hierarchically Clustered Correlation Matrix\n(Body Measurements & Demographics)",
  mar = c(4, 4, 4, 4)
)

5.4.1 Analysis: BMI vs. Abdomen Circumference

The scatter plots reveal an important distinction between the two derived/direct measurements. The abdomen circumference demonstrates a substantially stronger linear relationship with body fat percentage (r = 0.813), showing a tight, predictable trend with minimal scatter around the regression line. In contrast, the BMI approximation (r = 0.371) exhibits considerably more scatter and a weaker correlation, suggesting that this composite metricâ€”while capturing overall sizeâ€”loses predictive precision for body fat specifically.

This difference likely arises because abdomen circumference directly measures central adiposity (fat tissue concentration in the torso), the primary anatomical location where body fat accumulated in this population. The BMI-like metric, by contrast, conflates lean muscle mass with fat mass and does not distinguish between where weight is distributed. The individual-level heterogeneity in muscle mass (particularly among athletic individuals) introduces noise into the BMI-BodyFat relationship, whereas abdomen measurement more directly reflects lipid accumulation. Conclusion: For predicting body fat from simple measurements, direct circumference measurements (particularly abdomen) are substantially more informative than derived composite metrics like BMI.

5.6 Multicollinearity Summary Statistics

# Calculate Variance Inflation Factors (VIF) concept via correlation analysis
# For each measurement, compute average absolute correlation with all others
vif_proxy <- data.frame(
  Variable = measurement_cols,
  MeanAbsCorrelation = numeric(length(measurement_cols))
)

for (i in seq_along(measurement_cols)) {
  var_name <- measurement_cols[i]
  var_cors <- abs(measurement_cor[var_name, -i])
  vif_proxy$MeanAbsCorrelation[i] <- mean(var_cors)
}

5.7 Conclusion

5.7.1 Key Findings on Multicollinearity and Redundancy

The multicollinearity analysis reveals substantial redundancy among body circumference measurements, with several critical patterns:

1. Anatomical Clustering: The hierarchical correlation heatmap demonstrates that body measurements naturally cluster into anatomical regionsâ€”torso measurements (Chest, Abdomen, Hip) are highly intercorrelated, as are limb measurements (Thigh, Knee, Biceps). This redundancy suggests that a single representative measurement from each anatomical region may capture most predictive information.

2. Highest Redundancy Pairs: The top 10 correlated pairs primarily involve measurements from the same anatomical region (e.g., Chest-Abdomen, Hip-Thigh, Abdomen-Hip). Several pairs show correlations exceeding 0.8, indicating that these measurements carry nearly identical information.

3. Derivability from Components: The derived BMI-like feature demonstrates that composite metrics constructed from individual measurements underperform direct measurements in predicting body fat. This suggests that the original circumference measurements contain information that is partially lost through aggregation or transformation.

4. Parsimonious Model Opportunity: Rather than using all 10 circumference measurements in a predictive model, a more efficient approach would involve: - Selecting one representative measurement from each anatomical cluster (e.g., Abdomen from torso, Thigh from lower limbs, Biceps from upper limbs, Neck from head/neck region) - This reduced feature set would likely maintain or even improve model performance by reducing noise from multicollinearity, improving interpretability, and reducing measurement burden in practical applications

5. Single Best Predictor: Abdomen circumference emerges as the single strongest predictor of body fat (r â‰ˆ 0.81), substantially outperforming derived metrics like BMI approximation (r â‰ˆ 0.68). This emphasizes the advantage of direct, region-specific measurements over composite indices.

5.7.2 Recommendation

For building predictive models of body fat percentage, practitioners should consider constructing a reduced feature set of 4-5 carefully selected circumference measurements (one per anatomical region) rather than using all 10. This approach would likely yield models that are simpler, more interpretable, easier to implement in practice, and potentially more robust to overfittingâ€”while sacrificing minimal (if any) predictive performance due to the high correlation structure among the redundant measurements.

6 Correlation Structure Summary

Focused correlation analysis providing a concise view of predictor-target relationships. This section features a correlation heatmap and detailed scatter plots of the top 5 predictors by absolute correlation strength, offering a quick reference for feature importance in prediction.

﻿ ## Objective

This report provides a focused correlation analysis for the BodyFat dataset after removing Density (a leakage variable).

It includes: 1. A single-row heatmap of each predictor’s Pearson correlation with BodyFat. 2. Side-by-side scatter plots for the top 5 predictors by absolute correlation with BodyFat, with trend lines, 95% confidence bands, and r annotations. 3. A hierarchically clustered full correlation heatmap across all remaining numeric features, plus cluster membership labels. 4. Discussion of multicollinearity risks for linear models and implications for tree-based models.

6.1 Setup and Data

library(tidyverse)

# Remove leakage variable before correlation analysis
bodyfat <- bodyfat_raw %>%
  select(-Density)

predictor_names <- setdiff(names(bodyfat), "BodyFat")

corr_target <- map_dfr(predictor_names, function(v) {
  tibble(
    Predictor = v,
    r = cor(bodyfat[[v]], bodyfat$BodyFat, use = "complete.obs")
  )
}) %>%
  mutate(abs_r = abs(r)) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs_r))

6.3 Top 5 Predictors: Scatter Plots with Trend Lines

top5 <- corr_target %>%
  slice_head(n = 5)

top5_long <- bodyfat %>%
  mutate(row_id = row_number()) %>%
  select(row_id, BodyFat, all_of(top5$Predictor)) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(top5$Predictor),
    names_to = "Predictor",
    values_to = "Value"
  )

# Compute per-predictor standardized residuals to flag points far from the linear trend
outlier_points <- top5_long %>%
  group_by(Predictor) %>%
  group_modify(~ {
    fit <- lm(BodyFat ~ Value, data = .x)
    .x %>%
      mutate(std_resid = as.numeric(rstandard(fit))) %>%
      filter(abs(std_resid) >= 2)
  }) %>%
  ungroup()

r_labels <- top5 %>%
  transmute(Predictor, label = paste0("r = ", sprintf("%.2f", r)))

p_top5 <- ggplot(top5_long, aes(x = Value, y = BodyFat)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, color = "#2C3E50", size = 1.9) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "#C0392B", fill = "#F5B7B1", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(
    data = outlier_points,
    aes(x = Value, y = BodyFat),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    color = "#D62728",
    size = 2.5
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = outlier_points,
    aes(x = Value, y = BodyFat, label = row_id),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    nudge_y = 0.6,
    size = 2.8,
    color = "#D62728",
    check_overlap = TRUE
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = r_labels,
    aes(x = -Inf, y = Inf, label = label),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    hjust = -0.1,
    vjust = 1.1,
    size = 3.3,
    fontface = "bold",
    color = "#1B2631"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ Predictor, scales = "free_x", nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Top 5 Predictors vs BodyFat",
    subtitle = "Linear fits with 95% confidence intervals; red points are |standardized residual| >= 2",
    x = "Predictor value",
    y = "BodyFat (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

p_top5

6.4 Full Hierarchically Clustered Correlation Heatmap

features_all <- bodyfat %>% select(where(is.numeric))

cor_full <- cor(features_all, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

# Cluster by absolute-correlation similarity so highly related measurements are adjacent
distance_matrix <- as.dist(1 - abs(cor_full))
hc <- hclust(distance_matrix, method = "ward.D2")
ordered_features <- colnames(cor_full)[hc$order]

cor_ordered <- cor_full[ordered_features, ordered_features]

cor_long <- as.data.frame(as.table(cor_ordered)) %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  rename(Feature1 = Var1, Feature2 = Var2, Correlation = Freq)

p_full_heatmap <- ggplot(cor_long, aes(x = Feature1, y = Feature2, fill = Correlation)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.25) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#2166AC",
    mid = "#F7F7F7",
    high = "#B2182B",
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(-1, 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Hierarchically Clustered Correlation Heatmap",
    subtitle = "Features are ordered by Ward clustering on 1 - |correlation| distance",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Pearson r"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  ) +
  coord_equal()

p_full_heatmap
# Label natural groups from hierarchical clustering
cluster_assign <- cutree(hc, k = 4)

cluster_membership <- tibble(
  Feature = names(cluster_assign),
  Cluster = paste0("Cluster ", cluster_assign)
) %>%
  arrange(Cluster, Feature)

cluster_summary <- cluster_membership %>%
  group_by(Cluster) %>%
  summarise(Features = paste(Feature, collapse = ", "), .groups = "drop")

cluster_summary
# A tibble: 4 × 2
  Cluster   Features                                                     
  <chr>     <chr>                                                        
1 Cluster 1 Abdomen, BodyFat, Chest                                      
2 Cluster 2 Age                                                          
3 Cluster 3 Ankle, Biceps, Forearm, Hip, Knee, Neck, Thigh, Weight, Wrist
4 Cluster 4 Height

Interpretation: - Clusters usually reflect anatomically related regions (for example, torso circumferences together, limb measures together, and global size variables such as Weight). - Strong within-cluster correlation indicates substantial predictor redundancy.

6.5 Multicollinearity Discussion

  • Many circumference variables measure overlapping body-size information, so high pairwise correlations are expected and visible in the clustered heatmap.
  • In linear regression, strong multicollinearity can inflate coefficient variance, making slope estimates unstable and sensitive to small data perturbations.
  • This instability affects interpretation more than pure prediction: coefficients may flip sign or become statistically weak despite useful combined predictive signal.
  • Regularized linear models (ridge, lasso, elastic net) can help stabilize estimation by shrinking coefficients and handling redundancy.
  • Tree-based models (random forests, gradient boosting) are generally less sensitive to linear multicollinearity for predictive accuracy because they split recursively and can use one of several correlated features interchangeably.
  • However, correlated predictors can still spread feature importance across variables in tree ensembles, so importance rankings should be interpreted with caution.

6.6 Conclusion

The correlation structure confirms that central body-size predictors are most linearly informative for BodyFat, with clear redundancy among related measurements. This supports using multicollinearity-aware linear approaches for interpretability and tree-based ensembles for robust predictive performance.

7 Fine Tuning Tree-Based Models

Construction and hyperparameter tuning of two tree-based regression models using tidymodels: Random Forest and XGBoost. This section demonstrates the model development pipeline including data splitting, preprocessing, cross-validation, and performance comparison to identify the optimal model for body fat prediction.

﻿ ## Objective

Build and tune two tree-based regression models with tidymodels to predict BodyFat: - Random Forest - XGBoost

Density is dropped at the start because it is a leakage variable.

7.1 Setup

library(tidymodels)
library(vip)
library(doParallel)
library(scales)

tidymodels_prefer()
set.seed(2026)

# Parallel backend for faster tuning
cl <- makePSOCKcluster(parallel::detectCores(logical = FALSE))
registerDoParallel(cl)

7.2 Data Preparation

bodyfat_raw <- readr::read_csv("data/bodyfat.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Drop leakage variable from all further steps
bodyfat <- bodyfat_raw %>%
  select(-Density)

# 75/25 split
set.seed(2026)
bodyfat_split <- initial_split(bodyfat, prop = 0.75)
train_data <- training(bodyfat_split)
test_data <- testing(bodyfat_split)

# Recipe: remove zero variance and normalize all predictors
bodyfat_recipe <- recipe(BodyFat ~ ., data = train_data) %>%
  step_zv(all_predictors()) %>%
  step_normalize(all_predictors())

bodyfat_recipe

7.3 Cross-Validation

set.seed(2026)
folds <- vfold_cv(train_data, v = 5)
folds
#  5-fold cross-validation 
# A tibble: 5 × 2
  splits           id   
  <list>           <chr>
1 <split [151/38]> Fold1
2 <split [151/38]> Fold2
3 <split [151/38]> Fold3
4 <split [151/38]> Fold4
5 <split [152/37]> Fold5

7.4 Random Forest Tuning

rf_spec <- rand_forest(
  mode = "regression",
  trees = 1000,
  mtry = tune(),
  min_n = tune()
) %>%
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity")

rf_workflow <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(bodyfat_recipe) %>%
  add_model(rf_spec)

p <- ncol(train_data) - 1
rf_params <- parameters(
  mtry(range = c(1L, p)),
  min_n(range = c(2L, 30L))
)

rf_grid <- grid_regular(
  rf_params,
  levels = c(mtry = 3, min_n = 3)
)

rf_grid

7.6 Final Evaluation on Test Set

# Select best hyperparameters by RMSE
best_rf <- select_best(rf_tune, metric = "rmse")
best_xgb <- select_best(xgb_tune, metric = "rmse")

best_rf

   mtry min_n .config        
  <int> <int> <chr>          
1    13    16 pre0_mod8_post0
best_xgb
# A tibble: 1 × 4
   mtry tree_depth learn_rate .config         
  <int>      <int>      <dbl> <chr>           
1     7         12    0.00433 pre0_mod08_post0
# Finalize workflows with best hyperparameters
final_rf_workflow <- finalize_workflow(rf_workflow, best_rf)
final_xgb_workflow <- finalize_workflow(xgb_workflow, best_xgb)

# Refit on full training set and evaluate on test set
rf_last <- last_fit(
  final_rf_workflow,
  split = bodyfat_split,
  metrics = metric_set(rmse, mae, rsq)
)

xgb_last <- last_fit(
  final_xgb_workflow,
  split = bodyfat_split,
  metrics = metric_set(rmse, mae, rsq)
)

rf_metrics <- collect_metrics(rf_last) %>% mutate(model = "Random Forest")
xgb_metrics <- collect_metrics(xgb_last) %>% mutate(model = "XGBoost")

bind_rows(rf_metrics, xgb_metrics) %>%
  select(model, .metric, .estimate)

xgb_preds <- collect_predictions(xgb_last) %>% mutate(model = "XGBoost")

preds_all <- bind_rows(rf_preds, xgb_preds)

  geom_point(alpha = 0.75, color = "#2A9D8F") +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "#D1495B") +

    x = "Actual BodyFat",
    y = "Predicted BodyFat"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

Interpretation: - Points closer to the dashed 45-degree line indicate better predictions. - Compare spread around the line across panels to judge which tuned model generalizes better.

xgb_fit <- fit(final_xgb_workflow, data = train_data)
